idiom_name: external descriptor type + per-type bindings consumed by generic algorithms
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: name the property the algorithm needs, put that property in a descriptor whose members are the associated types, constants and operations for one type or family (never the type's own members), write the algorithm against the descriptor only, and let each type acquire the descriptor either intrinsically (it already exposes the members) or through a binding declared elsewhere (specialization, instance, conformance, token). Resolve the binding where the algorithm is instantiated, so selection happens without a common base class and, where the language allows it, without runtime dispatch; keep the descriptor stateless and let an undescribed type fail loudly rather than fall back to a guess. Where the language can state the requirement directly (constraints, concepts, type-class contexts, structural protocols), express it there and keep the descriptor only for the payload the constraint cannot carry.
code_sketch:
trait Descriptor[T]:                        # one property -> one descriptor
    associated Value; Reference; Category   # types and constants the algorithm needs
    op compare(a: T, b: T) -> Ordering      # operations the algorithm may call

# bindings are supplied OUTSIDE the types (never by inheritance):
bind Descriptor[Frame*] as PointerFrame
bind Descriptor[char]   as CharFrame

# generic algorithm names the descriptor, not the type's members:
for T where Descriptor[T]:
    total = fold(items, Descriptor[T].identity, Descriptor[T].combine)
pitfalls: Requiring the descriptor's members but never checking their meaning: a binding that compiles but returns the wrong answer is this pattern's characteristic silent failure.
Falling back to a guess for undescribed types instead of failing at the binding, which turns a missing description into a wrong result far from its cause.
Letting one descriptor accumulate every property of a type, so that a single changed property forces a full reimplementation of the binding.

Wrong move: adding the missing binding wherever the gap appears - implementing a foreign trait for a foreign type, an overlapping instance, a retroactive conformance of a third-party type to someone else's protocol -> Rust rejects the impl (E0117), GHC's incoherent instances let different modules resolve the same constraint to different code, and Swift's SE-0364 warns about exactly this -> instead declare the binding in the package that owns either the type or the trait; when you own neither, route through a newtype wrapper or a remote definition (serde's remote derive) instead of fighting the coherence rules.

Wrong move: probing for a member with a SFINAE detector or implicit-search fallback inside the generic body -> the algorithm silently takes the degraded path for any type that nearly matches, and every diagnostic points at the probe instead of the missing binding -> declare the required interface as an explicit constraint (concept, protocol bound, type-class context) so an undescribed type fails naming the requirement.

Wrong move: consulting the descriptor with an if at every micro-decision inside one generic body -> the algorithm decays into branch soup and the slow path still has to instantiate for every type -> let the descriptor select a whole implementation (tag dispatch, a specialized impl) so each path stays straight-line and testable on its own.
